transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood CSM); Nora Patel (CTO), Samir Rao (Platform Eng), Evelyn Wu (ML Infra), Jamie Li (SRE)

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on streaming p95 targets and burst readiness. Atlas wants a plan for predictable p95 under mixed streaming and non-streaming load, plus guidance on hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs and an initial benchmarking plan.

Topics:
- Current app architecture and traffic shape
- p95 latency targets and SLAs
- Concurrency and token/sec expectations (steady-state + burst)
- Streaming vs non-streaming path differences
- Dedicated capacity / VPC / on-prem considerations
- Security: SOC 2, KMS, audit logs
- Next steps: share prompts, run micro-benchmarks, pricing sketch

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena Park: all right everybody thanks for joining, uh we'll give it a hard cut at 40 minutes, just want to make sure we cover your p95 targets and the streaming bit. Nora, do you want to quickly frame the problem?
[00:22] Nora Patel: thanks, yeah, um hi everyone - we're Atlas Cognition. We've got a customer-facing agent that streams answers to users as they type and then also a longer batch generation step for reports. So two workloads: low-latency streaming for interactive, and high-throughput non-streaming for reports. We're seeing tail spikes on busy days and want to understand if Redwood Hosted will meet our p95 of 250ms for streaming tokens at 100 concurrent streams, or if we need Dedicated or Private.
[01:05] Marcus Chen: mm-hmm, okay. couple clarifying q's - when you say 100 concurrent streams is that 100 open socket connections where each stream is producing tokens at, say, 6-10 tokens/sec on average?
[01:20] Samir Rao: correct, average ~7 tok/sec during interactive periods, bursts up to 18 tok/sec for short periods when customers paste prompts. Our session length average is ~18 tokens generated before user edits, but report generation is 4k-8k tokens in non-streaming mode.
[01:45] Marcus Chen: got it. and what's your p95 definition — end-to-end observed latency from request to first token or per-token latency while streaming?
[01:55] Evelyn Wu: it's first-byte p95 — user should see the first streaming token under 250ms. subsequent tokens can be a bit looser but we don't want visible jitter.
[02:10] Lena Park: thanks. couple quick notes: hosted has the fastest onboarding and generally hits low latency for single-stream scenarios; Dedicated gives you predictable tail and throughput guarantees because you reserve GPU pools; Private is usually for strict compliance or very tight egress/residency needs. We'll walk tradeoffs.
[02:33] Jamie Li: on security — we are SOC 2 and soon ISO as well; we care about KMS integration and audit logs. If we go Dedicated or Private we want customer-managed KMS in the VPC.
[02:50] Diego Alvarez: noted, we do support KMS/HSM integrations for Private stacks and Dedicated with customer key options, and audit logs through the Console. I'll follow up with the security pack.
[03:04] Marcus Chen: so for a back-of-envelope we need to size token/sec per GPU and latency tradeoffs. A couple of internal notes: streaming latency is dominated by per-token model compute and the network hop; continuous batching can help throughput but sometimes increases first-byte latency if not configured carefully.
[03:28] Nora Patel: yeah that was our fear - batching to amortize cost might push the first token past 250ms. What are typical defaults?
[03:37] Marcus Chen: default hosted runtime aims to keep batching latency low - small micro-batches with dynamic batching. For 100 concurrent streams at ~7 tok/sec that's roughly 700 tok/sec aggregate steady-state. But the per-token CPU/GPU time depends on model size and quantization. What model are you planning to serve?
[03:58] Samir Rao: we want to use a 13B open model to start, maybe quantized 4-bit for cost. Later possibility to move to a 70B variant for specific customers.
[04:12] Marcus Chen: 13B quantized typically reduces GPU mem and speeds up per-token, but the exact tokens/sec per GPU varies across kernels. As a rough rule, a single A100/A10 equivalent instance in our Dedicated pool can sustain X tokens/sec for streaming on 13B — (note: placeholder) — we'll send the micro-bench numbers. For p95 first-byte under 250ms across 100 concurrent streams you'll likely need either: a) Hosted with autoscaling and region co-location plus prefix caching, or b) Dedicated with reserved slots to avoid noisy neighbors and guarantee concurrency headroom.
[04:48] Evelyn Wu: what's prefix caching?
[04:51] Marcus Chen: prefix or KV cache caches repeated initial KV cache states for identical or similar prompts — reduces compute for the early tokens and is great when prompts share common system + few-shot context. It needs consistent model versions and works best with Dedicated or Private where cache locality is stable, though hosted can also do it in many cases.
[05:10] Nora Patel: our prompts are fairly templated so caching seems promising. But we're also worried about burst paste events where many clients send long prompts simultaneously - report generation is separate but bursts happen across both.
[05:25] Marcus Chen: for burst paste we recommend a mixed routing policy: keep interactive routing to low-latency pool and route heavy long-form to a high-throughput pool to avoid tailing the streaming SLO. Redwood supports routing by request properties with automatic fallback to cheaper model variants if capacity constrained.
[05:45] Jamie Li: fallback — will that change output quality significantly for us? We have compliance about accuracy for certain customers.
[05:52] Lena Park: fallbacks are policy-driven; you can pin critical tenants to Dedicated and let non-critical requests use cost-optimized variants. We'll discuss canary rollout and A/B comparisons during the pilot.
[06:07] Samir Rao: can you talk more about the benchmarking plan? We want to validate p95 under our traffic shape end-to-end.
[06:16] Marcus Chen: yes — we recommend a two-stage bench: 1) Micro-bench per-model on Dedicated/hosted to measure raw tokens/sec and per-token latencies with your quantization settings. 2) End-to-end replay using your prompt set at scaled concurrency (using our benchmarking harness or your load generator) to measure first-byte p95 and token jitter. We'll share the micro-bench sheet and a script.
[06:40] Nora Patel: how long does the end-to-end take?
[06:44] Marcus Chen: a couple hours for a representative run, longer if you want sustained soak tests. For Dedicated we can also do a short smoke test in your reserved pool.
[06:55] Evelyn Wu: network hops — if we host in same cloud region will that shave 20-30ms?
[07:00] Marcus Chen: yes colocating in the same region reduces network latency significantly; typical cross-region add 40-80ms depending on the path. So placing Redwood endpoints in the same cloud region as your app is recommended for tight p95 targets.
[07:14] Nora Patel: what about TLS termination and websocket streaming? We use websockets for streaming.
[07:20] Marcus Chen: WebSockets are supported; keep-alive matters. TLS handshake latency only affects cold starts. Once the connection is open the per-token path is shorter. For p95 you'll want connection pooling and sticky sessions in front of your app.
[07:33] Jamie Li: any pitfalls with KV cache invalidation during model rollouts?
[07:38] Marcus Chen: yes rolling model versions can invalidate caches; we recommend canary and pinned sessions for critical flows. Redwood Console shows KV cache hit metrics so you can track regression.
[07:50] Nora Patel: on Dedicated sizing, if we need headroom for 100 concurrent streams but spikes to 300 for short windows, do you recommend overprovisioning or autoscale?
[08:00] Lena Park: a combination: reserved base capacity with autoscale burst is typical. Dedicated supports configurable autoscaling with burst credits; you commit to baseline and enable short bursts above it. Pricing/commit terms vary — I'll include options in the pricing sketch.
[08:15] Samir Rao: curious about real-world numbers — can you share a concrete example?
[08:19] Marcus Chen: sure, an internal example: a client using a 13B quantized model with streaming saw first-byte p95 ~180ms at 60 concurrent streams (avg 8 tok/sec) on hosted in region, and with Dedicated that same workload had p95 ~140ms and better tail consistency. But results are model- and kernel-dependent. We will provide a small matrix of numbers for 13B/70B across quant levels.
[08:46] Nora Patel: okay that helps. Regarding security: if we go Dedicated inside our VPC can we have customer-managed KMS and private peering?
[08:56] Diego Alvarez: yes, Dedicated can be deployed with VPC peering and customer-managed keys; Private on-prem is an option if you need full air-gap, but usually Dedicated with VPC is sufficient for most enterprise compliance.
[09:10] Evelyn Wu: do you have SLAs for p95?
[09:13] Lena Park: we have uptime SLAs for Dedicated and hosting tiers; p95 latency SLAs are usually part of the enterprise contract for Dedicated with specific targets and penalty clauses — we'll look at a proposal once we know your target and commit level.
[09:26] Nora Patel: perfect. On telemetry, we need per-token latency histograms and per-route traces.
[09:32] Marcus Chen: Console shows token-level breakdowns, route-level dashboards, traces, and error rates. We also expose tracing hooks to send to your observability stack.
[09:43] Jamie Li: who runs the pilot? we'd prefer Redwood SE then our SRE to run it together.
[09:48] Marcus Chen: happy to run with you. Typically SE (me) and CSM coordinate the test window and support. Diego will own the security doc delivery.
[09:58] Nora Patel: timeline — we want a pilot in 2-3 weeks and a production decision in 6 weeks.
[10:04] Lena Park: sounds reasonable. We'll send calendar invites for a pilot kickoff and provide the micro-bench sheet within 48 hours.
[10:12] Samir Rao: any network egress cost surprises for hosted?
[10:16] Diego Alvarez: egress is billed per cloud region per our pricing; if you keep things internal via VPC peering with Dedicated you can often reduce egress costs. We'll detail that in the pricing sketch.
[10:27] Nora Patel: about fallbacks: if Dedicated is saturated can you auto-fail to hosted without losing auth or data residency?
[10:36] Marcus Chen: policy-based failover is supported. Data residency concerns are owned by policy: you can choose to block failover for certain tenants or allow only to compliant regions. Auth tokens and audit logs are preserved but we can walk the specifics.
[10:51] Lena Park: quick recap and next steps — Marcus will drop the micro-benchmark spreadsheet, I'll send pricing sketch and Dedicated commit options, Diego will send security pack. Nora will provide prompt set and traffic histogram. We schedule pilot kickoff for two weeks.
[11:08] Nora Patel: sounds good thanks everyone.
[11:12] Jamie Li: thanks, appreciate the clarity.
[11:15] Lena Park: thanks all, talk shortly.

End of transcript.
